# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains almost everything about how municipal water systems work. A cubic foot of water weighs about 62 pounds, and a column of water only one inch square but ten feet tall already exerts over four pounds per square inch of pressure at its base. Engineers exploit this relationship constantly, and understanding it is the key to understanding how water gets from a reservoir to a seventh-floor shower head.

## The Fundamental Physics: Elevation as Pressure

The workhorse concept here is called "head" — hydraulic head, specifically. Every foot of elevation difference between a water surface and a faucet translates to roughly 0.433 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure. This is why cities historically built water towers and reservoirs on hills: elevation *is* energy. Water at 200 feet above a faucet delivers about 87 psi before a single pump is involved.

Consider a concrete example. Imagine a mid-sized city with its main reservoir sitting in hills 300 feet above the downtown core.
